articles.content:
Episode Description:

Most world maps show Greenland and Africa as roughly the same size… which is kind of unbelievable considering Africa is 14 times larger! This error has been built into classrooms, boardrooms, and institutions since 1569. Last week, 164 countries finally voted to fix it.

Arielle and Karissa also cover a solar ambulance built by university students that completed its first real-world test in rural Kenya, a student baking operation in Frisco, Texas that has raised over $8,000 for food-insecure kids, and why the best time to deal with weeds is probably right now.

Nominate a Local Changemaker (30 and under): https://us20.list-manage.com/survey?u=d2e7810fd2bcf24fb1144a7e2&id=6e0ab37520&e=28025b5010

If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com.

Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary.

Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram, X, and Blue Sky.

The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy.

Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d

Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes

Transcript:

Intro & Housekeeping

Arielle:

Hi, everyone. It’s Arielle.

Karissa:

And I’m Karissa.

Arielle:

And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s Weekly Roundup. How are you doing this- uh, this beautiful Friday, Karissa?

Karissa:

Doing great. It’s, it’s a beautiful Friday indeed. What about you, Arielle?

Arielle:

I’m doing well. I am excited for hopefully a less social weekend. I think as the summer winds down-

Karissa:

Mm-hmm

Arielle:

people are a little bit more introspective, and I’m gonna try to, um, to save my, my own energy and keep a little bit to myself-

Karissa:

Mm-hmm …

Arielle:

and do cozy things like crochet or watch a movie or curl up with a book or something like that.

Karissa:

Yeah. That’s exactly how I feel. I think finally I’m past so many of the summer weekends now that everyone’s kind of settling in this back to school, back to everything routine that- Mm-hmm

comes with September, I feel like. So I think this is my first free-ish weekend in a while myself, and I really need to start… I’m, I’m very determined to, uh, sew everybody something for Christmas presents this year, but I have to get started now, otherwise it’s gonna not happen. So I’m hoping this weekend I can sit down and get to work on that.

Arielle:

Oh, wow. Yeah, you did mention that you started sewing. Is that a new hobby, or?

Karissa:

Yeah. That’s a recent hobby for me, which is such a coincidence because we actually have a solution that we’ll share at the end about how great hobbies are for you.

Arielle:

Hmm. All right. Well, before we jump into the solutions, just a quick reminder, nominations are still open for our Local Changemaker series, which we do every year in the run-up to Thanksgiving.

Karissa:

And if you missed the update last week, we’re doing the whole Changemaker series this year on Changemakers 30 and under.

Arielle:

If you know someone, a young person making a positive impact in their community, nominate them. It’s a great way to practice your gratitude. The link to do that- Mm-hmm … is in the show notes, and it only takes two minutes.

Karissa:

And everyone who submits a nomination gets entered to win an Optimist Daily mug.

Arielle:

It’s honestly my favorite mug. It’s such a good mug. Mm-hmm. And we have decided on a closing date, so that’ll be Friday, October 2nd. So you still have a couple weeks to get your nominations in, but we’re excited to see who you guys introduce us to.

Karissa:

Absolutely. And just a reminder that we have a free daily and weekly newsletter that has all The Optimist Daily solutions included. If you wanna sign up for that, the link to do that is also in the show notes.

Arielle:

You can also follow us on socials. We are @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism.

Karissa:

And on socials you can reach out to us, say hi, share any comments, questions, or feedback, and you can also just email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We’d love to hear from you.

Arielle:

Mm-hmm. As usual, we would like to send a huge thank you to our financial supporters, our Emissaries. You guys help us keep this mission alive, and as a small thank you, we offer you The Optimist Daily shout-out perk.

If you haven’t taken advantage of that, the link to do that, we will be sending again soon. Uh, and that’s just an opportunity to shout out a local charity- A neighbor who helped you out with your gardening or something this weekend. Anybody that is just bringing positivity into your life. So it’s also another great way to share your gratitude for people.

Karissa:

Yeah, absolutely. Thank you so much to our Emissaries, but also a huge thank you to all of our Optimists for listening to the podcast, reading and sharing solutions, and just trying to spread some more optimism wherever you go, wherever you are. And with that being said, I think we should get into what went right this week.

Colombia’s Amazon Protection

Arielle:

I’m going to start us off with the first solution, “How Colombia’s outgoing president protected 42% of the country’s Amazon from mining”. Three days before a new president took office, and one who had campaigned on reviving oil drilling and legalizing fracking, Colombia’s outgoing president signed a resolution locking 186,500 square miles of the Amazon off from any new extraction.

On August 4th, 2026, President Gustavo Petro signed the resolution, and the incoming president, Abelardo de la Espriella, took office on August 7th. So they just squeezed that one in there, and now roughly 42% of Colombia is protected, and it’s the largest Amazon reserve ever created in the country.

Karissa:

A bold move to do that in such a tight window.

Arielle:

Yeah, I know. Definitely just trying to, like, get that last one in there before another president who has, uh, you could say, opposing values comes in.

Karissa:

Mm-hmm.

Arielle:

Um, but the legal mechanism behind this is Article 47 of the Natural Resources Code, which is a 50-year-old statute allowing the state to exclude an entire region from private exploitation.

It’s been used before, but only piecemeal. It never applied to the whole Colombian Amazon at once. This means that three things are now prohibited: new mining concessions, new oil and gas contracts, and the environmental permits that accompany either. Still, existing permits will continue until expiry, and there are a number of active mining titles and pending applications, and 39 active oil and gas contracts that all remain.

But the main thing is that they can’t be renewed.

Karissa:

Well, that’s good, and I hope that this solution will kind of stand in this transition of the powers here in the country, so…

Arielle:

Yeah, hopefully it, it holds. Um, but if it does, then Colombia would be of the strictest of the eight Amazon-sharing nations, which includes Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname.

Late Summer Weed Control

Arielle:

Moving on from the Amazon to people’s more personal, uh, little plots of greenery.

Karissa:

That’s right. Your own personal Amazon.

Arielle:

Yeah, that’s my transition. Uh, the next solution is titled “The gardening window most people miss: late summer and early fall weed control”. Most gardeners put away the hoe in late summer and consider it done until spring.

A professor of horticulture has a different take, though. What you do in these last weeks before frost shapes how much weed work you face next year. A single dandelion can drop thousands of seeds that stay dormant in the soil for years, so getting ahead of that in fall is easier than dealing with it in April.

The source behind this article is Manjot Kaur Sidhu, a horticulture professor at the University of Maine, and he says that right now, basically, is the single best time of year for weed control that lasts. I remember my dad just battling with weeds, like-

Karissa:

Yeah …

Arielle: basically my whole childhood. I don’t know if he ever won the war with weeds. So if you check out this article, maybe you have a chance.

The Mercator Map Resolution

Arielle:

The next solution is titled “The Mercator map has distorted Africa’s size for 450 years. The UN just voted to replace it.” On most world maps, Greenland and Africa look roughly the same size. Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometers.

Africa covers 30.4 million. The map has been wrong by a factor of 14 since 1569, and that error has been built into classrooms, conference rooms, and institutions ever since. 164 countries voted to fix that. So the UN General Assembly passed the Correct the Map resolution on September 5th, 2026. 164 nations voted in favor.

One voted against, which was the US, and then there were six abstentions. The resolution is sponsored by Togo and backed by the African Union’s 54 member states. It’s non-binding, but it’s still expected to drive changes to maps used by institutions worldwide. The Mercator map has been the global standard since 1569, and it was designed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.

I’m pretty sure that’s how you say it. Uh, although the Flemish have a different accent to the Dutch. He designed it to help European explorers navigate, and its distortion is a mathematical consequence of representing a globe on a flat surface. The map accommodates Earth’s curvature by making equatorial countries appear smaller and polar countries appear larger.

On the Mercator, Greenland and Africa look roughly the same size, as we mentioned before. Um, but yeah, it turns out that Africa is, like, 14 times larger, so it’s definitely not an accurate representation, let’s say. Yeah.

Karissa:

And as mentioned in this article, I mean, this map has implicitly downplayed Africa’s resources, population, and investment potential.

So it actually is really important that maps, you know, shape how regions are perceived politically and economically.

Arielle:

Mm-hmm. I really like the quote from the Togolese, um, foreign minister, Robert Dussey. Uh, he said, “A fair world begins with a fair map,” and I couldn’t agree more.

Elementic’s MO6 Carbon Tiles

Arielle:

All right, the next solution is called “Elementic’s MO6 is the building material claiming to lock away carbon for thousands of years”.

Lignin is the wood industry’s problem child. It comes off as a byproduct when timber is processed. It’s difficult to use, and it usually just gets burned for energy. A Finnish startup called Elementic decided to build a material out of it instead. The result is MO6, a wall tile made from 90% carbon that stores roughly twice the CO2 of wood and could keep it locked away for thousands of years.

This debut collection, MO6 Eternal, launched this month at Habitare in Helsinki as part of Helsinki Design Week. It’s a great use of this raw material that is usually considered too difficult to use. I like in this article that it kind of emphasizes that even though this is a really sustainable construction product, it’s being positioned more as a design object first and an environmental- Mm-hmm

product second, and then that framing changes who adopts it and how quickly they do that. So I guess it’s a little bit messed up that, like, people wouldn’t be more excited about, uh, an environmental product and that they’re more likely to adopt it if it’s seen as a design object, but this is just also a part of the strategy of creating a more sustainable world.

Karissa:

I took a look at these panels, and they’re pretty cool.

Arielle:

Yeah, they’re pretty sleek.

Karissa:

Yeah, they’re very sleek, so I could definitely see something like this in hotels, spas, restaurants.

Solar Ambulance in Kenya

Arielle:

All right. The last article that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand it over to Karissa is titled “The world’s first solar ambulance just completed its first real-world test in rural Kenya.”

Most ambulances are built around one question: How fast can we get the patient to a hospital? In regions without hospitals nearby, that question just doesn’t have a useful answer. Stella Juva, a solar-powered ambulance built by students at a Dutch university, takes a different approach. It shows up, it parks, it extends its solar panels out to the side for shade, and while it’s stationary, it generates more power than all of its medical equipment uses combined.

So this cool little vehicle was developed by Solar Team Eindhoven at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. Stella Juva is road legal, built as an electric vehicle with fully integrated solar panels, energy stored in a 50, uh, kilowatt hour battery, allowing operations after dark. It’s designed for remote regions that lack reliable infrastructure, electricity, and fuel options.

And unlike a traditional ambulance, it does not transport patients to hospitals, but rather brings healthcare directly to communities who need it.

Karissa:

And one thing this article kind of notes is how energy poverty is a healthcare barrier around the world that rarely gets discussed directly, because most global health coverage focuses on training, drugs, and facilities.

But power is the invisible constraint here.

Arielle:

And it was built by students, not a major medical device company. Mm-hmm. Which makes it, I think, even cooler. Um, I love a student-led technical innovation with real-world deployment. And yeah, the fact that the proof of concept came from a university team shapes what will happen next, and is also why our Local Changemaker series this year is based on younger innovators.

Baked Bites: Frisco Students

Karissa:

I’ll take it over from here. This one is called “Baked Bites: how Frisco students turned a passion for baking into a force for community change”. A group of students in Frisco, Texas started baking cookies to give back to their community. There wasn’t a GoFundMe involved, a sponsorship pitch, or a school project requirement.

They just homemade these baked goods, and sold through pre-orders and pop-ups, and every dollar is going directly to charity. They’ve raised over $8,000 for food insecure kids in their own school district, and the model, because it stays pretty simple, keeps working. Their Instagram handle is @bbaked_bites, and it operates through pre-orders and community pop-ups.

100% of proceeds go to charity, and there’s no overhead or admin cut taken by the organization. Their partner is Frisco Fastpacs, a nonprofit that delivers weekend meal bags to more than 1,200 food insecure children across Frisco ISD every Friday of the school year. For many of those kids, the bags are their primary source of food when school isn’t in session, so a really important initiative from their partner as well.

Karissa:

Like we mentioned, they raised $8,000-plus since launching, and the founders frame this as hundreds of people choosing kindness.

World’s Largest Electric Ferry

Karissa:

The next solution is “The world’s largest battery-electric ferry just crossed an ocean”. A ship ordered as a diesel ferry in 2019 became the largest electric vehicle ever built of any kind on land or sea.

It spent the pandemic getting redesigned from the ground up, then it crossed an ocean on the back of a heavy lift transporter to reach the river it was always meant to cross. The world record was not part of the original plan here, but it actually broke a world record. So this is Hull 096, which is named China Zorrilla in service, is a 130-meter, 427-foot battery-electric ferry built by Tasmanian shipbuilder Incat in Hobart.

It was originally ordered in 2019 as a diesel ferry by Buquebus, and it was redesigned to full battery electric propulsion during the pandemic production pause. It’s the largest electric vehicle of any kind on land or sea. It runs on more than 5,000 battery modules built from aluminum rather than steel to reduce weight and improve efficiency, and a full charge gives roughly 90 minutes of running time, which is just enough for its route.

Travel Scams to Watch For

Karissa:

The next solutions title is “Travel scams have gotten harder to spot. Here’s what changed and what to watch for.”. Summer travel is winding down, but before you put away the suitcase for good, it’s worth knowing that the scams targeting travelers have gotten significantly harder to spot. And with Thanksgiving and the holiday travel season a lot closer than it feels, now is a better time to think about this than at the airport gate.

The most dangerous travel scams today don’t really look suspicious. They actually look like a message you were already expecting. So this is just a great lifestyle solution that outlines a lot of scams that are out here. I mean, with the rise of AI tools, it’s made fake websites and communications substantially harder to detect.

So what used to look obviously fraudulent can now look really like routine correspondence. So-

Arielle:

Hmm …

Karissa:

lots of good tips in here, and honestly, a lot that I didn’t even know were going on, so I’m glad we reported on this. And-

Arielle:

Yeah …

Karissa:

according to an FTC report from June 2026, Americans lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams last year, and nearly one in three fraud reports involved an imposter.

Arielle:

Yeah, the reservation hi- hijacking one really freaked me out ’cause that’s the one that actually looks legit. Mm-hmm. Basically, the scammers will phish hotel staff for login credentials, and then they will access your real booking data and then contact you with your actual reservation dates and the exact cost.

So you’re, you feel like this has to be the actual hotel. Um- Hmm … and so your, your, like, walls of defense go down, and you just follow whatever they ask you to do. For instance, if they want you to click a link or something or send information. So yeah, that one was, was surprising to me, and the advice is just to go to the hotel’s official website and call the number before- Hmm

you do anything. I would probably fall for that, and I feel like I’m usually pretty vigilant when it comes to, um, parsing out the scams.

Karissa:

Yeah. Like you were saying with this one, Arielle, I mean, booking platforms are so confusing already, um , in my opinion. I mean, like I, I was staying at a hotel recently and I used a third party.

And I mean, it ended up being okay, but when I was checking in, the person was like, “Uh, can… Are you from Shanghai, China? That’s what it says your address is.” And I was like, “Oh, no.” And he was like, “Oh, did you book through a third party? ‘Cause it will, like, when- wherever the third party is based, it’ll populate as that address.”

So thing’s already confusing back there, and it can get even more confusing when people are trying to scam you.

Arielle:

Yeah, for sure.

Berlin’s Rooftop Farm Supermarket

Karissa:

The next solution we have is another really cool one in my opinion, and it’s “Berlin’s REWE supermarket: the grocery store with a working rooftop farm”. There’s a supermarket in Berlin where the lettuce on the shelf was growing on the roof just that morning.

The whole farm is built into the building, and it’s heated by waste heat from the refrigerators below, watered mostly by rain, and when the greens are ready, they come straight downstairs. There aren’t any trucks involved, distribution centers, or cold storage needed. It’s just a staircase. This REWE Lankwitz store in Berlin has a working rooftop with a hydroponic greenhouse, and the store was designed with the farm in mind from the start.

Skylights throughout the grocery floor let shoppers look up into what’s growing above them, and I think that is just such a cool concept and I wanna go to this grocery store. And I love all the circular systems that have been built into the building. Like I mentioned before, waste heat from the store’s refrigeration heats the greenhouse, and rainwater waters the plants, and solar provides additional power.

So this could definitely be the future of grocery stores.

Arielle:

Berlin is actually quite accessible to me. I have some friends there, so if I do end up visiting the supermarket, I will definitely let everyone on The Optimist Daily know. Um, and I just found it kind of eye-opening that, uh, this University of Groningen professor, Prajal Pradhan, published research that suggests that urban farming across Europe could supply up to 20 million metric tons of vegetables per year, and that’s around 28% of the continent’s total.

Uh, so that’s a pretty good chunk of our food security needs being met.

Karissa:

Hmm. Absolutely.

Low-Cost Hobbies for Joy

Karissa:

The final solution that I have to share is one that I mentioned at the beginning of the podcast. It’s titled “8 low-cost hobbies that add hours of joy to your week”. Research suggests that having an active hobby adds about eight hours of genuine satisfaction to your week.

Not just fun, but the kind of deep satisfaction that also improves mood, stress response, and maybe most surprisingly, immune function. This is a list of eight hobbies that cost almost nothing to start, and at least a couple of them are probably ones you’ve never tried. For a little research context, the research cited was pursuing a passion hobby can add eight hours of joy per week, and that’s defined as deep satisfaction, gratification, and accomplishment.

Evidence also links hobbies to better mood regulation, stress management, and immune function. So the physical benefit here tends to surprise people. I know it surprised me, but I’m glad because I’ve really been trying to engage more in my hobbies. And it’s also just a low-cost premise because hobbies that fit easily into daily life are the ones most likely to stick, and there are so many hobbies out there that cost very little or maybe even nothing to do.

So we won’t go into all eight of the hobbies that they suggest here, but of course, there’s way more than eight hobbies that, um, you can incorporate into your weekly routine. I think one that you probably won’t be surprised that I found interesting is journaling and junk journaling. So junk journaling, if you’re not familiar, is this recent, like, trend where you put a whole bunch of things you’ve found over the week, whether it’s ticket stubs, receipts, fabric scraps, magazine clippings, and you put them all into some tactile pages.

So it’s largely things that you already have, and it’s a cool way to, to recap what you’ve been and doing and use all the, quote-unquote, “junk” you found. One more that I’ve been taking part of a lot recently is hiking because I do have a lot of access to really awesome trails nearby. And I’ve been going with my group of friends, and we’ve kind of called it our, uh, girl gang hikes recently.

So it’s been a very fun hobby to take part in on the weekend, and we’ve seen- Oh, cute … a lot of cool things. Yeah, and, um, another important point of this article is just mentioning how incorporating, you know, bringing a friend to your hobby is a great way to, uh, have that social aspect, and it makes you more likely to stick with your hobby.

Arielle:

Hmm.

Closing Quote & Outro

Karissa:

Well, that’s all the solution news we had to share this week on The Optimist Daily. But before we leave, we’ll leave you with a positive quote that was featured in one of our daily newsletters this week.

Arielle:

I love this one. This is from Sandra Cisneros, who’s a… I believe she’s an American Chicana writer.

Um, the quote says, “The older I get, the more I’m conscious of ways very small things can make a change in the world. Tiny little things, but the world is made up of tiny matters, isn’t it?”

Karissa:

Mm. That one kind of gives me chills. I like that one- Yeah … a lot, ’cause it’s true, and I feel like that’s something we, we love to talk about on The Optimist Daily so much, is just how much our little collective actions can make the biggest difference.

So-

Arielle:

Mm. All right. Well, that’s a lovely note to end on. Karissa and I wish all of you Optimists and Emissaries and listeners out there a great weekend, um, and we will be back next week with more solutions.

articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant global event where 164 countries voted to correct a 450-year-old map distortion that misrepresents Africa's size, which has broad implications for political, economic, and educational perceptions worldwide. Additionally, it highlights other inspiring solutions such as Colombia protecting 42% of its Amazon rainforest, the world's first solar ambulance tested in Kenya, and sustainable innovations like carbon-locking building materials and urban farming. These stories collectively demonstrate meaningful, large-scale positive impacts on society and the environment with substantial context and detail.
articles.personality_title: 164 countries agree to fix 450-year-old map error showing Africa too small
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For centuries, many world maps have shown Greenland and Africa as similar in size, even though Africa is actually 14 times larger. This mistake started in 1569 with the Mercator map and has influenced how people see the world in schools, businesses, and governments.

**What happened** – On September 5th, 2026, the United Nations General Assembly voted on a resolution to correct this map distortion. 164 countries supported the change, while the United States voted against it and six countries abstained. The resolution was led by Togo and backed by the African Union’s 54 member states. The goal is to encourage institutions worldwide to update their maps to show Africa’s true size.

**Impact** – This correction is important because maps shape how people understand geography, resources, and power. The old map made Africa look smaller and less significant than it really is, which can affect political and economic decisions. Changing the map helps give a more accurate picture of Africa’s size and importance in the world.

**What’s next step** – Although the resolution is not legally binding, it is expected to influence schools, governments, and businesses to use more accurate maps. Over time, this could change how people learn about and interact with Africa and other parts of the world.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After 450 years, the world is moving to fix a map mistake that has made Africa look much smaller than it really is.
articles.personality_title_fr: 164 pays s'accordent pour corriger une erreur cartographique vieille de 450 ans sous-estimant l'Afrique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis des siècles, de nombreuses cartes montrent le Groenland et l'Afrique de taille similaire, alors qu'en réalité l'Afrique est 14 fois plus grande. Cette erreur date de 1569 avec la carte de Mercator et influence la façon dont le monde est perçu à l'école, au travail et en politique.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le 5 septembre 2026, l'Assemblée générale des Nations Unies a voté une résolution pour corriger cette déformation cartographique. 164 pays ont soutenu cette correction, les États-Unis ont voté contre, et six pays se sont abstenus. La résolution a été portée par le Togo et soutenue par les 54 membres de l'Union africaine. L'objectif est d'encourager les institutions à utiliser des cartes plus justes.

**Impact** – Cette correction est importante car les cartes influencent la compréhension de la géographie, des ressources et du pouvoir. L'ancienne carte faisait paraître l'Afrique plus petite et moins importante, ce qui peut influencer les décisions politiques et économiques. Changer la carte permet de mieux montrer la vraie taille et l'importance de l'Afrique.

**Prochaine étape** – Bien que la résolution ne soit pas contraignante, elle devrait encourager écoles, gouvernements et entreprises à adopter des cartes plus précises. Avec le temps, cela pourrait changer la façon dont les gens apprennent et interagissent avec l'Afrique et le reste du monde.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Après 450 ans, le monde s'engage à corriger une erreur cartographique qui a réduit faussement la taille de l'Afrique.
articles.personality_title_es: 164 países acuerdan corregir un error de 450 años que minimiza el tamaño de África
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante siglos, muchos mapas mundiales han mostrado a Groenlandia y África con tamaños similares, aunque en realidad África es 14 veces más grande. Este error comenzó en 1569 con el mapa de Mercator y ha influido en cómo las personas ven el mundo en escuelas, empresas y gobiernos.

**Qué pasó** – El 5 de septiembre de 2026, la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas votó una resolución para corregir esta distorsión del mapa. 164 países apoyaron el cambio, Estados Unidos votó en contra y seis países se abstuvieron. La resolución fue liderada por Togo y respaldada por los 54 estados miembros de la Unión Africana. El objetivo es animar a las instituciones a actualizar sus mapas para mostrar el tamaño real de África.

**Impacto** – Esta corrección es importante porque los mapas influyen en cómo las personas entienden la geografía, los recursos y el poder. El mapa antiguo mostraba a África más pequeña y menos significativa de lo que es realmente, lo que puede afectar decisiones políticas y económicas. Cambiar el mapa ayuda a dar una imagen más real del tamaño e importancia de África.

**Próximo paso** – Aunque la resolución no es vinculante, se espera que influya en escuelas, gobiernos y empresas para usar mapas más precisos. Con el tiempo, esto podría cambiar la forma en que las personas aprenden sobre África y otras partes del mundo.

articles.title: Berlin’s REWE supermarket: the grocery store with a working rooftop farm
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The lettuce in REWE’s Lankwitz store in Berlin has had a short morning. Grown on the rooftop farm directly above, cut, packaged by hand, and carried downstairs before most shoppers walk in, the whole trip from farm to shelf is measured not in miles but in flights of stairs. […]
The post Berlin’s REWE supermarket: the grocery store with a working rooftop farm first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

The lettuce in REWE’s Lankwitz store in Berlin has had a short morning. Grown on the rooftop farm directly above, cut, packaged by hand, and carried downstairs before most shoppers walk in, the whole trip from farm to shelf is measured not in miles but in flights of stairs.

The store was built with the farm in mind. Skylights throughout the grocery floor let you look up into what’s growing above. The greenhouse runs year-round on hydroponic technology, which means very little soil and a growing cycle of just over three weeks. It’s heated by waste heat from the store’s own cooling equipment, watered mostly by rain, and partly powered by solar. When the lettuce is ready, it comes straight downstairs.

A rooftop farm that works with the building

The waste heat from the refrigerators goes up to the greenhouse. The rain that falls on the roof waters the plants. Nothing leaves the building that the building doesn’t immediately use. The supply chain is a staircase.

Closing the gap between grower and shopper

“We don’t even have an extra truck on the road that usually is necessary to transport the goods from the producer to the central distribution,” said Leschke, the REWE project lead.

Prajal Pradhan, an associate professor at the University of Groningen who recently published a study on urban agriculture in Europe, has been thinking about the distance between producers and eaters for a while now. Projects like this one interest him. “There is a disconnection between producers and consumers,” he said. “This is a way to go forward, because you can provide fresh vegetables to urban consumers on site.”

The greens from Lankwitz aren’t just sold in this store, either. They go to other REWE locations across Berlin and the surrounding region, so the farm reaches more shoppers than the ones standing directly beneath it.

Rooftop farms and Europe’s vegetable supply

Pradhan and his colleagues looked at how much of Europe’s vegetable demand could realistically be met through rooftop and ground-based urban farming. The number they landed on is bigger than you might expect: up to 20 million metric tons (about 22 million US tons) per year, which is around 28 percent of the continent’s total. An earlier study by Pradhan found that Berlin alone could grow a significant share of its own vegetable needs within city limits.

Not a replacement for community gardens

Pradhan has one thing he wants people not to take away from all this: supermarket rooftop farms are not a substitute for community gardens. Urban agriculture should be inclusive, he says, and bring the whole neighborhood in, not just serve as a selling point for a retail chain. His co-author Stepan Svintsov, a remote sensing expert based in Berlin, put it this way: “Getting people together from a dense city and sharing agricultural knowledge among them helps bring the community together.” For now, REWE offers outside tours of the Lankwitz facility, but no one goes into the production rooms.

The plan to grow

Leschke wants to build at least 20 supermarket rooftop farms over the next 10 years, with at least one in every REWE region within five. “If we can produce in Germany year-round, we should,” he said. The draw, for him, is being less dependent on supply chains that stretch across the world.

Back at the display, a customer reaches for two bags of the Lankwitz lettuce. Another heads straight for the local variety, planning a tomato-and-mozzarella salad for later. She likes using the greenhouse greens, she says. After all, it came from the roof. And the roof is right there.

articles.title: Scientists just named a new snake after Guns N’ Roses legend Slash
articles.summary: A newly discovered snake from New Guinea has been named after Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash, who has loved reptiles since childhood. Genetic testing and physical differences confirmed that the reddish-brown groundsnake, Lielaphis slashi, is a species scientists had never formally recognized before. The nonvenomous snake may use large rear teeth to catch slippery lizards and reptile eggs.
articles.content:
Slash, also known as Saul Hudson, is famous worldwide as the guitarist for Guns N' Roses. But music is only part of his story. He has also been fascinated by reptiles for most of his life and has long supported zoos, museums, and natural history.

Now that passion has earned him an unusual scientific honor. Researchers have named a newly identified snake species from New Guinea Lielaphis slashi, or Slash's groundsnake.

"As a long time herpephile, I am extremely honored and humbled to have Lielaphis slashi from New Guinea named after me. It is really exciting, I never would have imagined this moment would arrive," says Slash.

A Childhood Connection to Slash

For Sara Ruane, the Field Museum's Associate Curator of Herpetology and senior author of a paper in Zootaxa describing the species, the name also has a personal connection.

"Guns N' Roses has been one of my favorite bands since I was in first grade, and by fifth grade, I had already told my teacher that I wanted to be a herpetologist -- a scientist who studies reptiles -- when I grew up," says Sara Ruane, the Field Museum's Associate Curator of Herpetology and senior author of a paper in Zootaxa describing the new species. "So when I was twelve years old and got my copy of Reptiles Magazine in the mail and it had a picture of Slash holding his pet reticulated python on the cover, I thought, 'This guy is so cool.'"

Years later, after Ruane became a scientist who sometimes has the opportunity to assign official names to newly recognized reptile species, she returned to that old magazine interview.

"I reread his interview, and he talked about how much he loves museums and zoos and natural history, and about how when he was a kid, he'd go outside and look for snakes -- it was all stuff that I really related to, and it made me think that he'd be a great person to name a new species after," says Ruane.

Her opportunity eventually came in the form of a reddish-brown snake measuring 28 inches long that had been collected in the forests of New Guinea.

A Mysterious Snake From New Guinea

New Guinea is the world's second-largest island, behind Greenland. Located just north of Australia, the island is divided between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea. Its tropical forests support enormous biological diversity, much of which remains poorly documented by scientists.

During fieldwork one night in 2006, Chris Austin, a professor and curator of herpetology at the Louisiana State University Museum of Natural Science, encountered a snake in New Guinea that he did not recognize.

"These New Guinea groundsnakes are nocturnal, so the best way to find them is at night. They are typically found just after sunset at the base of large trees where they are looking for something to eat," says Austin, a co-author of the paper describing the new species. "When working at night in New Guinea you need to be very careful as there are several highly venomous species that look very similar to the non-venomous groundsnakes."

After completing her doctorate, Ruane worked with Austin at LSU in 2016. The two began collaborating to better understand New Guinea's poorly studied snakes, and they have continued working together on the group ever since.

Genetics Reveal a New Species

At first glance, the snake did not obviously appear to represent a species new to science. Laboratory work, however, revealed important differences.

"Using multiple cutting-edge genetic analyses, we found that L. slashi is genetically distinct from other similar snakes in the same genus," says Tianqi Huang, the study's first author and a post-doctoral researcher at the Field Museum with Ruane. "The combination of physical characteristics, like differences in numbers of scales when compared with other species, and the genetic evidence is what led us to realize that it is an entirely new species. We also used ecological modeling to show that L. slashi's preferred habitat is different from similar snakes."

The researchers combined genetic evidence with physical traits, including differences in scale counts, to distinguish L. slashi from related snakes. Ecological modeling also indicated that the new species favors a different type of habitat than similar members of the genus.

What Slash's Groundsnake Eats

Scientists still know relatively little about the behavior and ecology of Slash's groundsnake.

"It's incredibly hard to observe snakes in the wild before they slither away, so our knowledge about L. slashi is limited," says Ruane.

Its anatomy does provide some hints about how it may live and feed.

"Snakes in this genus often have large teeth in the back of their mouths, which New Guinea groundsnakes may use to grab on to and eat small, slippery-scaled lizards and the eggs of other reptiles; this snake isn't grasping and squeezing its prey like a boa constrictor," says Ruane.

Although Guns N' Roses has been called the "most dangerous band in the world," its reptilian namesake is not dangerous to people. L. slashi does not produce venom capable of seriously harming a human.

Threats to New Guinea's Forests

Slash's groundsnake may pose little danger to humans, but human activity could threaten the species and many other animals living in New Guinea's forests.

"The habitats that Slash's groundsnake is from are under threat from industries like coffee farming and mining," says Ruane. "That's part of why describing the species that live there is important. Every species should be recognized in order for us to better understand how ecosystems work, how everything fits into the environment. We can't conserve animals or other living things that we don't know about."

By formally identifying species such as L. slashi, scientists can build a clearer picture of New Guinea's biodiversity and better understand which organisms may be at risk as their habitats change.

This study was contributed to by Tianqi Huang (Field Museum and Rutgers University), Chris Austin (Louisiana State University Museum of Natural Science), Justin Bernstein (Slippery Rock University and the American Museum of Natural History), Bulisa Iova (Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery), Jackson Roberts (Virginia Museum of Natural History), Jeffrey Frederick (University of Kentucky), and Sara Ruane (Field Museum).

articles.title: When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
articles.summary: A neighbourhood’s fight to save a cherished ginkgo pits them against an unlikely foe.
articles.content:
Every summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.

But this year, one tree was visibly suffering.

"Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul.

The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern.

A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo?

The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym.

"Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die.

"How heartbreaking would that be?"

So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist.
